full_title: SPOUSES NOEL M. AGULLO AND LENY AGULLO, AND JOSEPHINE BERMEJO, PETITIONERS, VS. LEA VICTA – ESPINOSA, REPRESENTED BY AURORA A. VICTA, RESPONDENT.
subject: Civil Law and Land Titles and Deeds

Nature of the action is determined by the allegations of the complaint
Motu proprio dismissal limited to the four grounds in Rule 9, Section 1

doctrine:
**An accion publiciana may be brought when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year in any case, or when the dispossession has lasted for one year or less in cases other than those mentioned in Rule 70 of the Rules of Court**, i.e., when there is no allegation of deprivation of possession by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth. The dispossessed party in such a case need not wait for the one-year period to lapse. The Court En Banc **clarified** *Heirs of Cullado v. Gutierrez* by holding that the action also lies when the dispossession has lasted for exactly one year. It also clarified *Martinez v. Heirs of Lim*: an accion reivindicatoria "can" (not "shall") be filed after one year; no one must wait a year before suing to recover ownership.

The nature of the action, and the court that has jurisdiction, are determined by the **allegations in the complaint**, not by later pleadings or motions. **A complaint that merely alleges the plaintiff's ownership and seeks to recover possession, without praying for recovery of ownership or annulment of title and without alleging that the defendant disputes the plaintiff's title, is an accion publiciana, not an accion reivindicatoria.** Not every encroachment case is an accion reivindicatoria. "Independently of title" means the better right of possession may or may not proceed from title. "Without claim of title" means there is no claim of title hostile to or inconsistent with the plaintiff's, or, if there is one, it is not alleged in the complaint. If ownership is raised only in the answer, the court in an accion publiciana may resolve it provisionally, and only to settle possession, where the two issues are inseparably linked.

Under **Rule 9, Section 1** of the Rules of Court, a court may dismiss a claim motu proprio only for (1) lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, (2) litis pendentia, (3) res judicata, or (4) prescription. Prematurity is not one of them (reiterated).
facts:
After buying a parcel of land, respondent Lea Victa-Espinosa had it surveyed and found that petitioner spouses Noel and Leny Agullo had encroached on a portion of it. The spouses refused her demand to vacate. She filed a Complaint for Recovery of Possession before the Regional Trial Court of Daet, Camarines Norte. The complaint alleged that she owns the land (assessed at PHP 68,060.00), that the defendants had encroached on it, that they had been illegally occupying it "long before the plaintiff acquired the same" as "mere informal settlers," and that they refused her demands to vacate. It prayed that they be ordered to vacate and to pay attorney's fees, moral damages and exemplary damages. It did not pray for recovery of ownership or annulment of title.

Without issuing summons, the RTC dismissed the complaint on August 5, 2019 as premature: an action for forcible entry could still be filed within one year from the discovery of the dispossession, and only after that may a recovery of possession case be filed. In her motion for reconsideration, respondent argued that her complaint was an accion reivindicatoria because she sought to recover ownership and possession as an attribute of it. The RTC denied the motion on October 4, 2019.

On certiorari, the Court of Appeals (March 17, 2023 Decision; September 25, 2023 Resolution, CA-G.R. SP No. 163854) set aside the RTC orders and ordered a trial on the merits. It held that the complaint was an accion reivindicatoria and that a boundary dispute or encroachment can be settled only in such an action. The spouses Agullo went to the Supreme Court under Rule 45. They argued that the complaint was an accion publiciana, which may be filed only when dispossession has lasted for more than one year, so the case was premature. Citing *Martinez v. Heirs of Lim*, they added that even an accion reivindicatoria may be filed only after more than one year of dispossession.
issues: Whether the RTC could dismiss the complaint motu proprio, before issuing summons, on the ground of prematurity.
Whether the complaint is an accion reivindicatoria or an accion publiciana.
Whether an accion publiciana may be filed only when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year.
Whether, under Martinez v. Heirs of Lim, an accion reivindicatoria may be filed only when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year.
ruling:
**1. No.** Rule 9, Section 1 allows a court to dismiss a claim motu proprio in only four instances: lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, litis pendentia, res judicata, and prescription. "Dismissal on the ground of prematurity is not one of them." The RTC erred procedurally.

**2. It is an accion publiciana; the CA erred in calling it an accion reivindicatoria.** The Court compared the complaint with the one in *Macutay v. Samoy*, captioned "Accion Reivindicatoria with Damages" but held to be an accion publiciana because it had no prayer for recovery of ownership or annulment of title. The present complaint likewise had no such prayer. Respondent's claim, made only in her motion for reconsideration and her CA petition, that she was seeking ownership did not count, because the nature of the action is determined by the allegations in the complaint, "not the allegations in a subsequent pleading or motion." There was no boundary dispute, and respondent did not allege that petitioners disputed her title, so there was no ownership for the court to determine conclusively.

The Court explained the source of the confusion. Accion reivindicatoria has been described as an action to recover possession "as an element of ownership." But a judgment in that action determines ownership and awards possession to the owner; it does not determine possession alone. "Mere averment or allegation of plaintiff's ownership, on its own, is not tantamount to seeking recovery of ownership or alleging dispute as to plaintiff's ownership." Conversely, describing accion publiciana as a suit for the better right of possession "independently of title" or "without claim of title" does not mean that a complaint alleging title cannot be an accion publiciana. "Independently of title" means the better right may or may not proceed from title. "Without claim of title" means no hostile claim of title, or none alleged in the complaint. In *Spouses Cruz v. Spouses Torres*, the defendants' claim of ownership surfaced only in the answer, and the action remained an accion publiciana. The court may still pass on ownership raised in the answer, but only provisionally and to resolve possession.

**3. No.** Both courts and both parties wrongly assumed that an accion publiciana may be filed only after more than one year of dispossession. In *Heirs of Cullado v. Gutierrez*, citing *Gumiran v. Gumiran*, the Court En Banc held that an accion publiciana may be filed even if dispossession has lasted for less than a year "in cases other than those mentioned in Rule 70," that is, when there is no allegation of deprivation by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth. **The Court clarified *Heirs of Cullado*: the action may also be filed when dispossession has lasted for exactly one year. "In sum, an accion publiciana may be brought when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year in any case, or when the dispossession has lasted for one year or less in cases other than those mentioned in Rule 70 of the Rules of Court."** Since the complaint was an accion publiciana and the assessed value alleged was within the RTC's jurisdiction under Republic Act No. 7691, the law in force when it was filed, it was properly filed with the RTC.

**4. No.** *Martinez* stated that an accion reivindicatoria "can be filed when the dispossession lasted for more than one year." The Court found that *Martinez* may have misquoted *Bongato v. Spouses Malvar*. *Bongato* meant only that once ejectment is no longer available because dispossession has lasted more than a year, the dispossessed party may still file an accion publiciana or reivindicatoria; hence "can be filed" and not "shall be filed." "To say that one must wait for a year to lapse before seeking recovery of ownership is simply absurd and defies logic and reason."
disposition: The Petition was DENIED. The Court of Appeals' March 17, 2023 Decision and September 25, 2023 Resolution in CA-G.R. SP No. 163854 were AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION: the complaint was declared an accion publiciana. The trial court was directed to conduct further proceedings with reasonable dispatch and decide the case on the merits.

bar_questions.q: Ana bought a titled lot in Camarines Sur. A relocation survey in March 2025 showed that Ben's house encroached on 80 square meters of the lot. Ben ignored Ana's written demand to vacate. In June 2025, Ana filed with the Regional Trial Court (the assessed value is within the RTC's jurisdiction) a "Complaint for Recovery of Possession." She alleged that she is the registered owner, that Ben occupies the encroached portion without right, and that he refused to vacate. She prayed that Ben be ordered to vacate and to pay damages. The complaint does not allege that Ben entered by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth, and it does not allege that Ben disputes her title. (a) What is the nature of Ana's action? (b) Ben moves to dismiss, arguing that the action is premature because less than one year has passed since Ana learned of the encroachment. Should the motion be granted?

alac.answer: (a) It is an accion publiciana, not an accion reivindicatoria. (b) No, the motion should be denied; the action is not premature.
alac.legal_basis: The nature of an action is determined by the allegations in the complaint. A complaint that alleges the plaintiff's ownership and seeks only to recover possession, with no prayer for recovery of ownership or annulment of title and no allegation that the defendant disputes the title, is an accion publiciana. An accion publiciana may be brought when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year in any case, or when it has lasted for one year or less in cases other than those mentioned in Rule 70 of the Rules of Court, i.e., when there is no allegation of deprivation of possession by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth. (Spouses Agullo v. Victa-Espinosa, G.R. No. 269921, April 22, 2025, En Banc)
alac.application: (a) Ana alleges ownership, but she prays only that Ben vacate and pay damages. She does not seek recovery of ownership or annulment of title and does not allege that Ben disputes her title. Her allegation of ownership alone does not turn the case into an accion reivindicatoria, and encroachment alone does not require one. The action is a plenary action to recover the better right of possession. (b) Her complaint does not allege dispossession by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth, so the case is not one of those mentioned in Rule 70. She does not have to wait for one year to lapse before filing an accion publiciana. Since the assessed value is within the RTC's jurisdiction, the RTC may take cognizance of the case.
alac.conclusion: Ana's complaint is an accion publiciana that was properly and timely filed, so Ben's motion to dismiss should be denied.

bar_questions.q: Carlos owns a farm lot. In February 2026 he discovered that Dante had secretly entered the lot at night two weeks earlier, fenced off a portion, and planted crops. In April 2026, Carlos filed with the Regional Trial Court a complaint captioned "Accion Publiciana." He alleged that Dante deprived him of possession by stealth and prayed that Dante be ordered to vacate. The assessed value of the lot is within the RTC's jurisdiction. Is the accion publiciana the proper remedy?

alac.answer: No. Because the complaint alleges dispossession by stealth and the dispossession has not lasted for more than one year, the case falls under Rule 70. The proper remedy is an action for forcible entry in the proper first-level court.
alac.legal_basis: Accion interdictal (forcible entry or unlawful detainer) is the summary action for recovery of physical possession where the dispossession has not lasted for more than one year, and it is brought in the proper inferior court. An accion publiciana may be brought when the dispossession has lasted for more than one year in any case, but when it has lasted for one year or less only in cases other than those mentioned in Rule 70, i.e., when there is no allegation of deprivation of possession by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth. (Spouses Agullo v. Victa-Espinosa, G.R. No. 269921, April 22, 2025, En Banc, applying Heirs of Cullado v. Gutierrez)
alac.application: Unlike a complaint that is silent on the manner of entry, Carlos's complaint expressly alleges that Dante entered by stealth, a ground mentioned in Rule 70. The dispossession has lasted only a few months. The one-year period for forcible entry, counted in cases of stealth from the time the owner learned of the entry, has not lapsed. The exception allowing an accion publiciana within one year does not apply. The caption "Accion Publiciana" does not control; the allegations do.
alac.conclusion: Carlos should file a forcible entry case in the proper first-level court, not an accion publiciana in the RTC.

bar_questions.q: Elena filed with the Regional Trial Court a complaint for recovery of possession of her lot against Fidel. Before summons was issued, the RTC dismissed the complaint motu proprio as "premature," reasoning that Elena should first wait for the one-year period for forcible entry to lapse. (a) Was the motu proprio dismissal proper? (b) On what grounds may a court dismiss a claim on its own initiative?

alac.answer: (a) No, the motu proprio dismissal was improper. (b) Only for lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, litis pendentia, res judicata, or prescription.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 9, Section 1 of the Rules of Court, a court may dismiss a claim motu proprio only when it appears from the pleadings or the evidence on record that (1) it has no jurisdiction over the subject matter, (2) there is another action pending between the same parties for the same cause (litis pendentia), (3) the action is barred by a prior judgment (res judicata), or (4) the action is barred by the statute of limitations (prescription). In Spouses Agullo v. Victa-Espinosa (G.R. No. 269921, April 22, 2025, En Banc), the Court held that an RTC erred in dismissing a complaint for recovery of possession motu proprio, before issuing summons, on the ground of prematurity, because "[d]ismissal on the ground of prematurity is not one of them."
alac.application: The RTC dismissed Elena's complaint on its own, before summons, solely for prematurity. That is not one of the four grounds in Rule 9, Section 1. The RTC's premise was also wrong, because an accion publiciana may be filed even before one year has lapsed when the complaint does not allege dispossession by force, intimidation, threat, strategy, or stealth.
alac.conclusion: The RTC could not dismiss Elena's complaint motu proprio for prematurity, because a court may do so only for lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, litis pendentia, res judicata, or prescription.

notes: The decision does not state the date the complaint was filed or exactly when the encroachment was discovered. It says the RTC dismissed the complaint as premature because forcible entry could still be filed within one year from discovery. The Court held the RTC had jurisdiction under RA 7691, "the prevailing law at the time of filing"; it did not discuss the thresholds under RA 11576. Josephine Bermejo is named as a petitioner, but the decision's narration refers only to the spouses Agullo.
